South Africa recorded 18 confirmed and one probable Monkeypox (mpox) case as of Thursday. The Department of Health on Friday said most infections are concentrated in Cape Town. Cases climb sharply in Western Cape Departmental spokesperson Foster Mohale said the country was seeing a fast rise in laboratory-confirmed infections. “The Department of Health is urging citizens to remain vigilant of mpox symptoms as the country is experiencing a rapid increase in laboratory-confirmed mpox cases in the past few weeks,” he said. Fifteen of the cases came from the Western Cape, mainly Cape Town, three from Gauteng, and one from KwaZulu-Natal. Read more Health department assures public that Enalapril 5mg remains safe despite 10mg recall Mohale noted that most infections were recorded within a five-week window. “Of concern is that 13 of the total cases were recorded between 13 August and 17 September, which suggests a rapid local transmission of this preventable viral infection,” he said. Patients ranged from 23 to 50 years old, with a median age of 36.5, and 18 of the 19 cases involved men. One recent patient had travelled to Spain and returned to South Africa on 14 September after testing there. Authorities said they were working with Spanish officials to confirm his status. RELATED ARTICLES Ramaphosa appoints Stella Ndabeni-Abrahams as acting health minister Good news in SA’s fight against TB Symptoms and how the virus spreads Mohale described mpox as a disease that does not discriminate. “Mpox is a viral disease that can affect anyone regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, and socioeconomic status,” he said. Symptoms include fever, fatigue, and skin lesions that progress from red spots to fluid-filled blisters and eventually crusted scabs, typically appearing six to 13 days after exposure. The virus spreads mainly through close physical contact, contaminated bedding or clothing, and prolonged face-to-face contact. “Hand hygiene through frequent washing or use of sanitisers is one of the effective methods to prevent the spread of the virus,” Mohale said. Read more How prepared is South Africa for a potential Ebola outbreak strain with no vaccine? Vaccines secured, public urged to avoid stigma With support from the World Health Organisation (WHO) the government has secured limited doses of the Tecovirimat vaccine. Mohale appealed for compassion toward affected people. “Stigma and discrimination have the potential to undermine an outbreak response by deterring people from seeking medical care,” he said. By SAPeople Staff Writer 18-09-26 08:38 in Health 0 Image: Wikipedia Commons South African health authorities have intensified surveillance and port screening after recording a rapid rise in mpox cases across the Western Cape, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal between 13 August and 17 September. Of the total confirmed cases, 15 were identified in the Western Cape – primarily in Cape Town – alongside three in Gauteng and one in KwaZulu-Natal. Patients range from 23 to 50 years old with a median age of 36.5 years, comprising 18 men and one woman. The Department of Health is also tracking an infection linked to international travel from Spain. How is South Africa responding to rising cases? To contain potential imports and local spread, the Border Management Authority has introduced thermal scanning and health declarations at ports of entry. “We are also in close collaboration with the communicable disease facilities in the districts in order to respond swiftly and ensure immediate reporting of any suspected traveller that meets the Mpox disease symptom profile,” said Border Management Authority Commissioner, Michael Masiapato. Meanwhile, the Department of Health has secured limited doses of the Tecovirimat vaccine through World Health Organization support to disrupt mpox transmission chains. Health officials emphasised that vaccination must complement frequent hand hygiene, while warning that social stigma deters vulnerable individuals from seeking early medical care. Key facts about mpox virus Cause and Symptoms: Caused by the monkeypox virus (Orthopoxvirus genus), mpox presents with fever, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, and painful skin lesions. Transmission: Spreads through close skin-to-skin contact, respiratory droplets during face-to-face interaction, or contaminated linens. Lefty Shivambu/Gallo Images The health department says that at least 18 new cases of mpox have been reported. Fifteen of those cases have been recorded in the Western Cape. The department said that a limited number of vaccines are available in the country. At least 18 new mpox cases have been reported, the Department of Health has said, with most of them centred in the Western Cape. The department added that, as of Thursday, the country has recorded 18 confirmed and one probable case. “The Department of Health is urging citizens to remain vigilant of mpox symptoms as the country is experiencing a rapid increase in laboratory-confirmed mpox cases in the past few weeks,” spokesperson Foster Mohale said. “This requires immediate and sustained public cooperation to contain.” ADVERTISEMENT The majority (15) of these cases were reported in the Western Cape, particularly in Cape Town. Three cases were reported in Gauteng and one in KwaZulu-Natal. “Of concern is that 13 of the total cases were recorded between 13 August and 17 September, which suggests a rapid local transmission of this preventable viral infection,” said Mohale. READ | Mpox outbreak in Africa was neglected, and could now turn into the next global pandemic The patients range in age from 23 to 50 years, with a median age of 36.5 years, and 18 of them are males, with only one female. ADVERTISEMENT “One of the most recent cases involved an individual who travelled to Spain earlier this month and returned to South Africa on 14 September. This person underwent testing in Spain after being informed of his probable case status. South African health authorities are in contact with the Spanish counterparts regarding laboratory test results of the individual to confirm his mpox status,” said Mohale Mpox may present in a person who was in close contact with someone who tested positive for the virus in the last few weeks (up to 21 days) and will present with similar symptoms. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue, and rash or skin lesions that may appear on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or other body parts. Typically, the skin lesions start as flat red spots, then progress to bumps, followed by fluid-filled blisters, then pus-filled bumps, and finally crusting over into scabs. READ | Mpox cases rise to 13, as health department receives first batch of disease-specific medication The symptoms usually appear within six to 13 days after exposure, but can range from 5 to 21 days. Mpox is transmitted mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact with the rash or lesions, and contact with contaminated materials such as bedding, clothing, or towels used by an infected person. Mpox-positive people can also transmit the virus through respiratory droplets during prolonged face-to-face contact, uncovered coughing or sneezing. “The government, through the support of the World Health Organisation, has secured limited doses of mpox vaccines (Tecovirimat) as part of its outbreak response strategy to disrupt local transmission. The health authorities will decide where and how to use these doses to contain outbreaks. Vaccination should be accompanied by continued adherence to preventive measures,” said Mohale. Editor BizNews Published on: 20 Sept 2026, 3:23 pm Copied Follow Us A permanent global mpox vaccine stockpile has launched, meant to let countries request doses within 48 hours of an outbreak rather than negotiating after the fact. Financed by Gavi and run through the International Coordinating Group, it marks progress after the scramble seen during the 2024 emergency. But the mechanism's real test comes once demand outstrips supply. South Africa has recorded eight cases in 2026, mostly in the Western Cape, and began targeted vaccination in Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape last year. With most of the global caseload in Africa, how doses are allocated will matter directly here. By Prof Colleen Aldous The next test of global vaccine equity has already started, and this time we cannot say we were taken by surprise. Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is a viral infection related to smallpox that can cause fever, a characteristic rash and, in some cases, severe illness. At the end of August 2026, a permanent global stockpile of mpox vaccines was launched. It was expected to begin operating during September 2026 and is intended to allow countries confronting outbreaks to obtain vaccines rapidly rather than negotiating for doses after an emergency is already under way. On the face of it, this sounds like a sensible piece of public-health administration. It may prove to be much more important. The stockpile provides an opportunity to find out whether global health has learnt one of the central lessons of recent epidemics. When medical products become scarce, principles of equity are much easier to proclaim before an emergency than to apply during one. Mpox has certainly not disappeared. The World Health Organization reports that between January 2022 and 31 July 2026, 145 countries and territories recorded 190,683 laboratory-confirmed cases and 529 deaths. Approximately two-thirds of currently reported cases are occurring in Africa. Mpox can cause severe disease, particularly in young children and people whose immune systems are compromised. South Africa is not removed from this picture. According to the National Institute for Communicable Diseases, eight cases had been reported in this country during 2026 by 28 August: six in the Western Cape and one each in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal. Four involved clade Ib virus and four clade IIb virus. South Africa began a targeted mpox vaccination programme in July 2025 in Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, where most cases have occurred. These are not mRNA vaccines One point is worth clarifying because the word “vaccine” now often immediately evokes the controversies surrounding COVID-19 vaccines. The principal mpox vaccines are not mRNA vaccines. MVA-BN, marketed under names including Jynneos, Imvanex and Imvamune, is based on Modified Vaccinia Ankara, an attenuated vaccinia virus related to the virus historically used for smallpox vaccination. It has been weakened so extensively that it cannot replicate in human cells. LC16m8 is another attenuated vaccinia-based vaccine. Unlike MVA-BN it can replicate to a limited extent and produces a characteristic local vaccination reaction. Both technologies arise from the long history of smallpox vaccination rather than the mRNA platform used for some COVID-19 vaccines. The evidence is encouraging, although it should not be overstated. The WHO reports that current studies suggest that people receiving two doses of MVA-BN have about an 82% lower risk of developing mpox than unvaccinated people, while one dose is associated with about a 76% lower risk. These estimates come largely from observational evidence generated during outbreaks rather than from the sort of large placebo-controlled efficacy trials familiar from some other vaccines. Safety surveillance is continuing. More than a million MVA-BN doses have been administered, and the WHO's vaccine-safety committee has reported a generally favourable safety profile, while acknowledging that information remains more limited in groups such as young children, pregnant women, immunocompromised people and populations outside Europe, North America and Australia. That is how vaccine evidence should be discussed. Neither as unquestionable certainty nor as evidence-free experimentation. The WHO does not recommend indiscriminate mass mpox vaccination. Vaccination is targeted towards people at increased risk during outbreaks, including close contacts, people in areas with substantial transmission and healthcare or laboratory workers with occupational exposure. The more interesting question now is not simply whether these vaccines work. It is who gets them when there are not enough to meet every request. Building the stockpile before the crisis The new system is being financed by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and managed through the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. The ICG is not a new organisation created for mpox. It has managed emergency vaccine stockpiles for diseases including cholera, yellow fever, meningitis and Ebola. Mpox becomes the fifth disease covered by this mechanism. Any country experiencing an outbreak will be able to apply for vaccines. Countries eligible for Gavi support will receive the vaccines without charge and may also receive assistance with implementation. Wealthier countries will be able to obtain vaccines just as rapidly, with Gavi initially financing the doses, but they will subsequently have to reimburse their cost. When a country applies, technical experts representing the WHO, UNICEF, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies will examine the epidemiological situation, the population proposed for vaccination, the strategy for delivering the vaccines and the number of doses requested. The intention is to reach an allocation decision within 48 hours. This is a significant improvement on trying to design an allocation mechanism after countries have already begun competing for scarce supplies. But the real test lies ahead. The precise size and composition of the mpox stockpile have not yet been announced. And that is important to know. Equity is relatively easy when there is enough vaccine for everybody who needs it. Allocation becomes ethically difficult when several countries face significant outbreaks simultaneously and available supply cannot satisfy them all. Imagine that one country has the largest number of cases, another has rapidly accelerating transmission, and a third has fewer cases but a large population particularly vulnerable to severe disease. Which should receive the doses first? Or suppose one country can distribute 100,000 doses within days while another has a much weaker health system and will require substantially more logistical support. Should preparedness determine priority? There is a defensible argument that scarce vaccines should go where they can be deployed rapidly and prevent the most infections. But there is an equally important danger. If “readiness” becomes too powerful an allocation criterion, countries with the weakest health systems may repeatedly find themselves at the back of the queue precisely because their health systems are weak. Efficiency and equity are not always the same thing. Africa has heard promises about vaccine equity before This question has particular resonance for Africa. The continent currently carries most of the reported mpox burden. Most of the vaccine manufacturing capacity required to respond lies elsewhere. During the 2024 mpox emergency, an ad hoc Access and Allocation Mechanism had to be created to distribute vaccines. International partners purchased or donated millions of doses, and vaccines began reaching affected African countries. Gavi acknowledges that the earlier global experience demonstrated the need for a more predictable system in which access did not depend primarily on a country's purchasing power. Creating a permanent stockpile in advance is therefore progress. But a global stockpile should not become a substitute for strengthening African capacity. Africa still needs better diagnostic capacity, surveillance, clinical services, regional procurement and vaccine manufacturing. A continent that continually depends on an international body to release emergency supplies remains vulnerable even when that body behaves impeccably. The same principle applies within countries. Vaccines sitting in an international warehouse do not control outbreaks. They must arrive quickly, reach the populations at highest risk, be accepted by communities and be incorporated into surveillance, diagnosis, contact tracing and clinical care. Vaccination is one component of mpox control, not the whole response. The real test comes when supply is tight The new stockpile deserves cautious support. It is better to secure vaccines before an epidemic escalates than to scramble for donations afterwards. It is better to have publicly defined mechanisms for allocation than to allow purchasing power alone to determine who receives scarce medical products. The establishment of a mechanism is not proof that equitable allocation has been achieved though. When the first substantial competing requests arrive, we should watch closely. Which countries apply? How many doses do they request? How many do they receive? What criteria determine the decision? How long does delivery take? Are populations at highest risk actually vaccinated? And when requests exceed supply, who goes without? Those data should be public. Transparency is essential because equitable allocation is not simply a technical exercise performed by experts. Decisions about scarce lifesaving resources inevitably contain value judgements about whose need is greatest and where intervention is likely to achieve the greatest benefit. COVID-19 showed how quickly declarations of international solidarity can weaken when countries fear that their own populations may go without. Read more: Prof Colleen Aldous: Measles is moving through South Africa. Is our response moving with it? Mpox gives the global health system another opportunity. This time the mechanism is being built before the emergency reaches its worst point. The vaccines already exist. The organisations responsible for allocating them are known. The rules are being established in advance. This is progress. But vaccine equity will not be demonstrated by the existence of a stockpile. It will be demonstrated by what happens when there are not enough doses for everyone who needs them. *Prof Colleen Aldous, Professor and Health Care Researcher Sign up for your early morning brew of the BizNews Insider to keep you up to speed with the content that matters. Read the article The Department of Health is urging the public to stay vigilant following a rapid rise in laboratory-confirmed Mpox cases. Advertisement Scroll to continue Department spokesperson Foster Mohale says that as of Thursday, 18 cases have been confirmed, with one probable case awaiting results. He says authorities are particularly concerned about the recent acceleration in cases. Most cases are in the City of Cape Town, while Gauteng recorded three cases and KwaZulu-Natal, one. Mohale says the patients are aged between 23 and 50, and only one patient is female. Travel-linked case under investigation One of the most recent cases involves a person who travelled to Spain earlier this month and returned to South Africa on 14 September. The individual was tested in Spain after being informed that they were a probable mpox case. Mohale says South African health authorities are engaging with their Spanish counterparts regarding the laboratory results to establish the person’s mpox status. The Department said the development highlights the importance of continued surveillance and early detection, particularly as cases can occur in people who have been in close contact with an infected person. What are the symptoms of mpox? Mpox is a viral disease that can affect anyone, regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation or socioeconomic status. The Department of Health urged people to be alert for symptoms including: Fever Headache Muscle aches Back pain Fatigue A rash or skin lesions The lesions can occur on the face, hands, feet, genitals or other parts of the body. Typically, the lesions begin as flat red spots before developing into bumps, followed by fluid-filled blisters and pus-filled bumps. These may eventually rupture and form crusted scabs. Symptoms generally appear within six to 13 days after exposure, although the incubation period can range from five to 21 days. Anyone experiencing symptoms, especially after close contact with someone who has a confirmed or suspected mpox infection, should seek medical attention promptly and avoid close contact with others. How does mpox spread? Mpox is transmitted primarily through close physical contact with an infected person. This includes skin-to-skin contact with mpox rashes or lesions, as well as contact with contaminated materials such as bedding, clothing and towels used by an infected person. The virus can also spread through respiratory droplets during prolonged face-to-face contact, including through uncovered coughing or sneezing. The Department said vigilance is particularly important in households, healthcare settings and close social networks. Regular hand hygiene — including frequent handwashing or the use of hand sanitiser — is among the measures that can help prevent transmission. Limited vaccines and treatment secured The government, with support from the World Health Organisation (WHO), has secured limited quantities of the MVA-BN mpox vaccine and Tecovirimat, an antiviral treatment, as part of the country's outbreak response. Health authorities will decide where and how to deploy the available doses to help contain outbreaks and disrupt local transmission. The Department stressed that vaccination should be accompanied by continued adherence to measures aimed at preventing transmission. Health Department warns against stigma Authorities are also urging communities to support people diagnosed with mpox, as well as those suspected of having the virus. The Department warned that stigma and discrimination could undermine efforts to control the outbreak by discouraging people from seeking medical care, testing or reporting symptoms. With cases increasing rapidly in recent weeks, the Department is calling for continued public cooperation, surveillance, and early detection to prevent further transmission. Members of the public who develop symptoms consistent with mpox, particularly following close contact with a confirmed or suspected case, should seek medical attention and avoid close contact with others while awaiting assessment. 359 Shares Previous Article Social development owes almost R18 million in rent on leased Sassa facilities 17 Sep Next Article Motorsport community mourns Robert Wolk after fatal road-rage shooting 18 Sep Most Read 118-year-old Centane woman honoured as living treasure EC Government delivers R42m ex-miner payout Bay woman missing, last seen on 1 September 2026 Shein valued at $26.3 bn in Hong Kong market debut Stolen e-bikes recovered in Wells Estate -GQ NERSA approves new Nelson Mandela Bay electricity tariffs Top Pick The Big C Podcast Series The Big C Podcast Series – brought to you by Algoa FM’s Big Walk for Cancer – takes a powerful step ALGOA FM NEWS EXCLUSIVE Journey to Justice, an exclusive podcast on the life of Vicki Terblanche, a slain Gqeberha mother. He said members of the public are reminded of mpox symptoms, which include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and rash or skin lesions that may appear on the face, hands, feet, genitals or other body parts. “Typically, the skin lesions start as flat red spots before progressing to bumps, followed by fluid-filled blisters, then pus-filled bumps and eruptions into crusted scabs.” The symptoms usually appear within six to 13 days after exposure but can range from five to 21 days. “Therefore, anyone experiencing these symptoms, particularly if they have had close contact with a confirmed case or a suspected case, should seek medical attention immediately and avoid close contact with others.” How mpox spreads Mpox is transmitted mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact with the rash or lesions, and contact with contaminated materials such as bedding, clothing or towels used by an infected person. Mpox-positive persons can also transmit the virus through respiratory droplets during prolonged face-to-face contact, uncovered coughing or sneezing. supplementary_news.content: News Health South Africa records 18 confirmed Mpox cases — TimesLIVE UA.NEWS 18 September 2026 09:59 As of September 17, South Africa had registered 18 laboratory-confirmed and one probable case of Mpox. Most cases were detected in the Western Cape province, primarily in Cape Town, TimesLIVE reports , citing South African Health Department spokesperson Foster Mohale. Most cases are in Cape Town According to the department, 13 cases out of the total were recorded between August 13 and September 17. Mohale said this indicates rapid local transmission of the viral infection. Fifteen cases were detected in the Western Cape, including Cape Town, three in Gauteng, and one more in KwaZulu-Natal. The patients are aged between 23 and 50, with a median age of 36.5 years. Of the 19 confirmed and probable patients, 18 are men and one is a woman. Case checked after travel to Spain One of the recent cases concerns a person who travelled to Spain this month and returned to South Africa on September 14. The person was tested in Spain after being notified of their probable-case status. South African health authorities are in contact with their Spanish counterparts regarding laboratory test results to confirm this person's status. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Mpox can develop in people who have had close contact with a person who tested positive for the virus during the past 21 days. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle and back pain, fatigue, a rash or skin lesions on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or other parts of the body. Health authorities' recommendations The virus is transmitted mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact with rashes or lesions, as well as through contaminated bedding, clothing, or towels. Transmission is also possible through respiratory droplets during prolonged face-to-face contact, coughing, or uncovered sneezing. People with relevant symptoms are advised to seek medical care immediately and avoid close contact with others. Frequent handwashing or the use of hand sanitizers was described as an effective way to prevent the virus from spreading. South African authorities, with support from the World Health Organization, have secured a limited number of Tecovirimat doses to respond to the outbreak; health authorities are to determine where and how they will be used. supplementary_news.content_title: The cause of 2022's mpox outbreak revealed
supplementary_news.content: CONTINUE TO SITE >> Instrumentation Equipment Computing Lab fit-out R & D Business Connect The Magazine Events Videos Resources Products Business Directory About Us Life Scientist Subscribe Magazine Subscribe eNewsletter The cause of 2022's mpox outbreak revealed Wednesday, 16 September, 2026 A research team led by the University of Surrey has discovered that the strain of mpox behind the 2022 outbreak was a weakened form of the virus, which may have helped it to spread faster. Their findings have been published in the journal Nature Communications. Mpox is a viral infection which causes flu-like symptoms and leads to the development of a blistering rash. The virus is a member of the orthopoxvirus family, which also includes the now-eliminated smallpox. The World Health Organization has twice declared mpox a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) — the highest alert level for an extraordinary global health event. “Outbreaks of mpox across the globe are becoming more common and continue to cause concern amongst populations in regions affected,” said Professor Maluquer de Motes, who led the new study. “The virus has established human-to-human transmission chains and the dangers it poses cannot be underestimated. “Although a vaccine is now in existence, supply chain issues remain and it is often a logistical challenge to ensure those who are most at risk are vaccinated. The best form of defence is to arm ourselves with as much knowledge about the virus and how it is evolving.” The study saw scientists analyse the mpox strain (Clade IIB, lineage B.1) which infected over 100,000 people in 120 countries in 2022 and compare it to an ancestral form of the virus (Clade IIB, lineage A.1) from which it derived. The scientists found that the genetic variation between the viruses was minimal, with only 46 nucleotides differing between the two out of a possible 197,000 nucleotides. This small differentiation ultimately resulted in the 2022 strain being less severe than lineage A.1, with a reduced ability to disseminate between cells. “Compared to other viruses, the genetic composition of mpox is huge,” de Motes said. “Typically having a difference of 46 nucleotides would not warrant such a change in the behaviour of a virus; however, this is not the case with mpox.” The scientists found that these variations were not caused by virus replication errors, but by enzymes in the human body, known as APOBEC3. As the virus circulated in humans, the enzymes introduced mutations that weakened the virus. For example, the 2022 strain induced higher levels of the protein IFNβ, a protein that acts as the body’s frontline defence against viruses. It also showed a reduced ability to suppress signals from proteins responsible for decreasing inflammation. The scientists found that the 2022 strain was less aggressive to the overall health of laboratory mice, who limited virus dissemination more effectively and had an increased survival rate after exposure to this strain compared to lineage A.1. The scientists thus theorise that the mutations may have helped the virus spread globally, as a weakened form of the virus would have enabled patients to continue with everyday life, interact with others and unknowingly spread the virus. “We were very fortunate that the 2022 outbreak of mpox contained the mutated strain of the virus, which we have found is less severe than its ancestors,” de Motes said. These mutations are however absent in current circulating forms of the virus in parts of Africa. “The quick spread of the virus across borders and amongst people exposes the dangers of mpox and how we are not yet fully equipped to deal with another outbreak of a viral infection.” Image credit: iStock.com/Berkay Ataseven Related News Heart muscle regeneration genes mapped Researchers have uncovered insights into how stem cells develop and mature into heart muscle... supplementary_news.content: Share current article via Email Share current article via Facebook Share current article via Twitter Share current article via LinkedIn Health officials urge vigilance as Mpox cases surge, with most infections reported in Cape Town. Picture: A rapid increase in laboratory-confirmed Mpox cases has been recorded in the past few weeks. Department of health spokesperson Foster Mohale said that by September 17 the country had recorded 18 confirmed and one probable case. “This requires immediate and sustained public co-operation to contain. ”Of concern is that 13 of the total cases were recorded between August 13 and September 17, which suggests a rapid local transmission of this preventable viral infection. “The majority (15) of the cases were reported in the Western Cape, City of Cape Town in particular, three in Gauteng and one in KwaZulu-Natal.” The patients range in age from 23 to 50 years, with a median age of 36.5 years, and 18 of them are males with only one female. One of the most recent cases involved an individual who travelled to Spain earlier this month and returned to South Africa on September 14. This person underwent testing in Spain after being informed of his probable case status. South African health authorities are in contact with their Spanish counterparts regarding laboratory test results of the individual to confirm his Mpox status. Mpox cases may present in any person who was in close contact with someone who tested positive for the virus in the last few days (up to 21 days) and will present by displaying similar symptoms. Mohale said: “The importance of continued surveillance, early detection, and public co-operation cannot be overemphasised in preventing further transmission.” Mpox symptoms include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and rash or skin lesions that may appear on the face, hands, feet, genitals or other body parts. Typically, the skin lesions start as flat red spots before progressing to bumps, followed by fluid-filled blisters, then pus-filled bumps and eruptions into crusted scabs. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should seek medical attention immediately and avoid close contact with others. Mpox is transmitted mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact with the rash or lesions, and contact with contaminated materials such as bedding, clothing or towels used by an infected person. Mpox-positive persons can also transmit the virus through respiratory droplets during prolonged face-to-face contact, uncovered coughing or sneezing. Hand hygiene through frequent washing or use of sanitisers is an effective method to prevent the spread of the virus. The government, through the support of the World Health Organisation, has secured limited doses of Mpox vaccines (Tecovirimat) as part of its outbreak response strategy to disrupt local transmission. Mohale said the health authorities will decide where and how to use these doses to contain outbreaks. TimesLIVE

supplementary_news.content_title: Mpox cases rise as Cape Town records majority
supplementary_news.content: Cape Town has recorded the majority of South Africa’s confirmed Mpox cases, with the Health Department urging the public to remain vigilant as infections continue to increase. The latest figures, highlighted by eNCA, show that 18 cases had been confirmed by Thursday, with one additional probable case also reported. Of the confirmed infections, 15 were recorded in Cape Town, while three were identified in Gauteng and one in KwaZulu-Natal. The figures point to a recent increase in cases, with 13 of the confirmed infections reported within a single month. Health authorities are now encouraging people to remain alert to possible symptoms and seek medical attention if they develop signs associated with the virus. Those diagnosed range in age from 23 to 50 years. Mpox can present with several symptoms, including; - Fever - Headaches - Muscle aches - Back pain - Fatigue. A rash or skin lesions are among the more recognisable symptoms and can develop on areas including the face, hands and feet, as well as elsewhere on the body. Mpox is primarily transmitted through close physical contact with someone who has the infection. Transmission can also occur through contact with contaminated materials. Items such as bedding, clothing and towels can carry the virus if they have been exposed to an infected person. Understanding how the virus spreads remains an important part of reducing the risk of transmission, particularly as health authorities monitor the recent increase in cases. supplementary_news.content_title: Mpox on the rise across the country, one case identified in KZN
supplementary_news.content: THE Department of Health is calling on citizens to remain vigilant as Mpox cases continue to rise within the country, with one person identified with the disease in KZN. Also read: KZN ready for possible monkeypox outbreak, says Health MEC There are 18 active cases of Mpox, with one case being probed. All patients range between 23 and 50 years and 18 of them are men while one is female. The latest case The most recent case of the virus was from a person who traveled to Spain and returned to South Africa on September 14. “Mpox cases may present in any person who was in close contact with someone who tested positive for the virus in the last few days (up to 21 days) and will present by displaying similar symptoms,” said the department in a statement. What is Mpox? Mpox is a viral infection that can cause painful rashes, fever, headaches and swollen lymph nodes. The virus is caused by the Monkeyvirus and is from the same family as smallpox. Symptoms and signs The department of health warns that the symptoms usually appear within 6 to 13 days after exposure but can range from 5 to 21 days. Common symptoms include: Rash Fever Sore throat Headache Muscle aches Back pain Low energy Swollen lymph nodes. “Typically, the skin lesions start as flat red spots before progressing to bumps, followed by fluid-filled blisters, then pus-filled bumps and eruptions into crusted scabs,” said the department. Transmission Mpox is a viral infection and is transmitted through close physical contact with an infected person. The World Health Organisation (Who) said that close contact, which includes skin-to-skin, mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-skin contact with someone who has Mpox, can put you at risk. The virus is also transmittable through contaminated clothing and linen, and by being bitten by an infected animal. If you are pregnant, it can be passed on to the baby. Vigilance is key The Department of Health is encouraging citizens to wash and sanitise their hands frequently as a precautionary measure. They have, through the support of Who, managed to secure a few vaccines that will be used at their discretion to ultimately stop the transmission of the virus. supplementary_news.content_title: Mpox alert: Western Cape traces contacts after cases linked to two gatherings
supplementary_news.content: News City Watch Opinion Lifestyle Sport Entertainment News Mpox alert: Western Cape traces contacts after cases linked to two gatherings Staff Reporter|Published 1 day ago Ask AI Health officials are tracing contacts after two Western Cape gatherings were linked to mpox cases. Image: File Western Cape Health officials are trying to track down people who attended two gatherings in the province after people infected with mpox came into close contact with others. The warning comes as the Western Cape accounts for 15 of South Africa’s 18 confirmed mpox cases, with most of the province’s infections recorded in Cape Town. “There were two events, exposure events, that basically did lead to these Mpox cases,” Western Cape health department official Ednah Baloyi said. Health teams are now tracing people who were at the gatherings, testing those who may have been exposed and making sure anyone who tests positive receives treatment. “We are working very hard to make sure that those two clusters are, or rather the contacts that were involved in that exposure event are followed up, tested, and treated timeously when they’re found to be Mpox positive,” Baloyi said. Symptoms to watch for The new details come as health authorities try to stop further infections following a sharp increase in cases over the past month. South Africa had recorded 18 confirmed cases and one probable case by September 17. Thirteen cases were recorded between August 13 and September 17, an increase the National Department of Health said pointed to the virus being passed between people locally. Those affected are between 23 and 50 years old. Western Cape health officials are urging residents to watch for an unexplained rash, sores or skin lesions, particularly if they have been in close contact with someone who may have mpox. Other symptoms can include fever, headaches, muscle aches and tiredness. Mpox is mainly passed through close physical contact with an infected person, including contact with their skin lesions, scabs or body fluids. The virus can also be picked up from items such as bedding, clothing and towels used by an infected person. Vaccines and treatment available Anyone who develops symptoms has been advised to avoid close physical contact with others and seek medical attention. Western Cape Health Chief Operating Officer Dr Saadiq Kariem said people who suspect they may have mpox should get medical help rather than wait for symptoms to worsen. South Africa has also secured limited supplies of the MVA-BN mpox vaccine and the antiviral treatment Tecovirimat with support from the World Health Organization. Vaccines are being given according to a person’s risk and whether they have been exposed to the virus, while people who test positive are advised to isolate until their skin lesions have healed. Mpox Western Cape Health Department Cape Town FILE: Mpox virus particles, illustration. Picture: SERGII IAREMENKO/SCIENCE PHOTO L / SIA / Science Photo Library via AFP Western Cape health authorities are ramping up surveillance and vaccination efforts as Mpox infections rise in the province. South Africa has recorded 18 confirmed cases since January, 15 of them in mainly in Cape Town. The provincial Health Department said that it’s working with the National Institute for Communicable Diseases, and the World Health Organization to strengthen surveillance and response to new cases. The department’s Chief Operating Officer, Dr Saadiq Kariem, said that vaccines are available based on a person’s risk and exposure. He’s also urging people to watch for symptoms, including fever, swollen glands and unexplained rashes, sores, or skin lesions. "Anyone can get Mpox, but what matters is knowing the signs, understanding how it spreads and then taking steps to protect the people around you. If you develop symptoms, please avoid close contact with people and also seek healthcare advice as soon as possible." Mpox Department of Health The backs of the hands of a patient with mpox showing a characteristic rash during his recovery phase. Picture: BSIP via AFP South Africa has recorded a rapid rise in mpox cases, with 18 confirmed infections and one probable case. The Western Cape has recorded 15 confirmed cases, while three are in Gauteng and one is in KwaZulu-Natal. ALSO READ: WHO declares mpox a global health emergency Mpox epidemic disinformation debunked Mpox cases rise in DR Congo as country awaits vaccines Thirteen of the cases were recorded between 13 August 2026 and 17 September 2026, suggesting rapid local transmission. Mpox is mainly spread through close physical contact with an infected person or contaminated materials such as bedding, clothing and towels. The department says anyone with symptoms, particularly after close contact with a confirmed or suspected case, should seek medical attention and avoid close contact with others. Department of Health spokesperson Foster Mohale explained. “Mpox is a viral disease that can affect anyone regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation and socioeconomic status. Members of the public are reminded of mpox symptoms, which include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and rash or skin lesions that may appear on the face, hands, feet, genitals or other body parts.” Never miss a major story. The department’s Foster Mohale noted that as of Thursday, 17 September, 18 confirmed cases have been recorded, with one probable case of mpox. “One of the most recent cases involved an individual who travelled to Spain earlier this month and returned to South Africa on 14 September. This person underwent testing in Spain after being informed of his probable case status. South African health authorities are in are contact with the Spanish counterparts regarding laboratory test results of the individual to confirm his mpox status,” said Mohale. 15 of those confirmed cases come from the Western Cape, particularly in Cape Town. Two others were recorded in Gauteng and one in KZN. “All cases/patients range in age from 23 to 50 years, with a median age of 36.5 years, and 18 of them are males with only 1 female.” Mohale said this requires immediate and sustained public collaboration to contain further spread of the virus. “Of concern is that 13 of the total cases were recorded between 13 August and 17 September, which suggests a rapid local transmission of this preventable viral infection.” Mohale reiterated that Mpox can affect anyone and usually develops 5–21 days after exposure. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, and a rash or skin lesions that progress from red spots to bumps, blisters, pus-filled lesions and scabs. It spreads mainly through close physical contact, contaminated items, and prolonged face-to-face exposure. He said anyone with symptoms, particularly after contact with a confirmed or suspected case, should seek medical attention promptly and avoid close contact with others. supplementary_news.content: Monday, September 21, 2026 Menu #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Search #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Menu South African govt raises alarm over rising mpox cases, calls for public vigilance South Africa’s Department of Health urged citizens to watch for mpox symptoms as the country has seen a rapid rise in laboratory-confirmed cases in recent weeks. Ahmed Oluwasanjo • September 18, 2026 PATIENTS WITH MPOX(credit: the Guardian) South African authorities have raised the alarm over rising mpox cases, urging the public to stay vigilant to prevent wider spread of the disease. In a statement on Friday, South Africa’s Department of Health urged citizens to watch for mpox symptoms as the country has seen a rapid rise in laboratory-confirmed cases in recent weeks. “As of 17 September 2026, the country has recorded 18 confirmed and one probable case, and this requires immediate and sustained public cooperation to contain,” the statement said. “The majority (15) of these cases were reported in the Western Cape, City of Cape Town in particular, 3 in Gauteng and 1 in KwaZulu-Natal,” it added. Expressing concern over the rapid spread of mpox, the Department of Health said it recorded 13 of the cases in less than a month. “Of concern is that 13 of the total cases were recorded between 13 August and 17 September, which suggests a rapid local transmission of this preventable viral infection. All cases/patients range in age from 23 to 50 years, with a median age of 36.5 years, and 18 of them are males with only 1 female. “One of the most recent cases involved an individual who travelled to Spain earlier this month and returned to South Africa on 14 September. This person underwent testing in Spain after being informed of his probable case status,” the statement added. According to the statement, South African health authorities are in contact with their Spanish counterparts to confirm the individual’s mpox status based on laboratory test results. “Mpox cases may present in any person who was in close contact with someone who tested positive for the virus in the last few days (up to 21 days) and will present by displaying similar symptoms,” it added. Warning the public to be alert, authorities said continued surveillance, early detection, and public cooperation cannot be overemphasised in preventing further transmission. “Mpox is a viral disease that can affect anyone regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation and socioeconomic status. Members of the public are reminded of mpox symptoms, which include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and rash or skin lesions that may appear on the face, hands, feet, genitals or other body parts,” it added. Image: CDC Home » News » South Africa records rise in mpox cases, most in Western Cape South Africa records rise in mpox cases, most in Western Cape South Africa has recorded 18 confirmed mpox cases as health officials raise concern over a sharp rise in infections in recent weeks. By Tarryn-Leigh Solomons Published Sep 18, 2026 in News 0 Mpox can cause a distinctive rash or raised skin lesions, which may appear on the hands, arms and other parts of the body. Image: CDC South Africa has recorded 18 laboratory-confirmed mpox cases and one probable case, with most infections reported in the Western Cape. The Department of Health raised concern after 13 of the 19 confirmed and probable cases were recorded between 13 August and 17 September. Department spokesperson Foster Mohale said the increase suggests rapid local transmission and urged the public to remain alert for symptoms. ADVERTISEMENT Number of cases Of the 19 cases under the department’s count, 15 are in the Western Cape, mainly Cape Town, three are in Gauteng and one is in KwaZulu-Natal. The patients are between 23 and 50 years old, with a median age of 36.5. Eighteen are men and one is a woman. One of the most recent cases involves a person who travelled to Spain earlier this month and returned to South Africa on 14 September. The person underwent testing in Spain after being informed of their probable case status. South African health authorities are awaiting the laboratory result from their Spanish counterparts. What is mpox? Mpox, previously known as monkeypox, is an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus. It can spread from person to person through close physical contact, including skin-to-skin contact, as well as through contact with infected bodily fluids or contaminated objects. ADVERTISEMENT While many people recover within a few weeks, the illness can become severe in some cases, particularly among people with weakened immune systems. What are the symptoms of mpox? Mpox symptoms can include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and a rash or skin lesions. The lesions can appear on the face, hands, feet, genitals or other parts of the body. Symptoms generally develop within five to 21 days after exposure. The virus spreads mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact with lesions. It can also spread through contaminated items such as bedding, clothing and towels. The department urged anyone who develops symptoms, particularly after contact with a confirmed or suspected case, to seek medical attention and avoid close contact with others. supplementary_news.content: Share Your Friday top stories | Ekurhuleni suspect’s nationality unconfirmed, Mpox cases rise, Mapisa-Nqakula grilled on: Latest 20 September 2026 16:40 Municipal elections: EFF takes campaign to Cape Town Local Government Elections Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) City of Cape Town Julius Malema 20 September 2026 16:10 Family of missing SA journalist Micah Reddy pleads for his safe return Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) 20 September 2026 15:35 IFP says its fileding young people ahead of local govt elections Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) Local Government Elections Your Friday top stories | Ekurhuleni suspect’s nationality unconfirmed, Mpox cases rise, Mapisa-Nqakula grilled Johannesburg Eyewitness News 18 September 2026 | 7:44 Catch up on news of the suspect linked to the Ekurhuleni murders, the rise in SA’s cases of Mpox, and Mapisa-Nqakula’s ongoing legal woes. Top stories The nationality of a suspect linked to one of the Ekurhuleni murders might not be South African, though police are yet to identify which one it could be. Meanwhile, a rapid rise in Mpox cases has been recorded in South Africa, with 18 confirmed infections – most of these in the Western Cape. And in the courts, embattled former National Assembly Speaker Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula faced a grilling in the Pretoria High Court related to meeting with a questionable defence force contractor. Ekurhuleni murders: Police yet to confirm nationality of suspect linked to 1 case Police are yet to identify the nationality of the suspect arrested in connection with one of the nine murders in the City of Ekurhuleni. Deputy National Police Commissioner Tebello Mosikili said they have information that the person is not a South African. For the full article, click here. SA confirms Mpox cases rise to 18 South Africa has recorded a rapid rise in mpox cases, with 18 confirmed infections and one probable case. The Western Cape has recorded 15 confirmed cases, while three are in Gauteng and one is in KwaZulu-Natal. For the full article, click here. Corruption-accused Mapisa-Nqakula grilled over meeting questionable contractor Corruption-accused former National Assembly Speaker Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula has faced tough questions in the Pretoria High Court. She quizzed about meeting defence force contractor Nombasa Ntsondwa-Ndhlovu even after being warned about her. For the full article, click here. Urgent bid to halt eviction of more than 500 residents in Tshwane in court The Pretoria High Court will on Friday morning hear an urgent application by Lawyers for Human Rights to stop the eviction of more than 500 residents from the Melgisedek building in Tshwane. The High Court ordered the eviction in March, and the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) dismissed the residents’ challenge last week. For the full article, click here. DJ Warras murder case: Alleged mastermind expected to finalise legal representation The alleged mastermind in the murder of musician Warrick "DJ Warras" Stock is expected back in the Johannesburg High Court on Friday morning to finalise his legal representation ahead of the trial. Victor Majola is expected to appear alongside a newly arrested woman, 40-year-old Hlengiwe Buthelezi, who was arrested in Msinga, KwaZulu-Natal, last week. For the full article, click here. National Assembly unsure how US visa restrictions will impact MPs serving in govt The National Assembly’s presiding officers don't know what the impact of the new United States (US) visa restrictions will be, and how they will affect the country’s members of Parliament (MPs) who also serve in government. National Assembly Speaker Thoko Didiza and her deputy, Dr Annelie Lotriet, said they can only wait and see how far the restrictions will go in targeting government ministers and their families over the country's transformation laws.
